A few hours ago, I got into a conversation with a person about the new EU regulations which she heralded as the best thing to happen for privacy in a long time. She made some points which I liked, seeing I hate big corporations and the government slowly gobbling up my personal data like some kind of black holes. Anyway, she linked me to the location here

https://archive.fo/5QwG7

Once I looked into it, I started doubting how much good it would do, but I still compiled this list. This is in no way comprehensive of what is on the site I linked, just whatever points of data I could gather over the course of an hour or so before becoming burned out and losing interest since this doesn't directly apply to me that much. All points are taken from layman level summaries, not the actual legislation, so there may be discrepancies between points I make and how the law actually works.

Anyway, here is what I came across in a nicely formatted list of pro's and con's. Quotes are what the document said, everything else is my comments. Sorry if it is hard to read.

Pros

Single law replaces multiple other laws, saving time and legislative hassle (and supposedly $2.3 billion Euros, though that is a small number on the scale of an entire superstate. How did they come to this number anyway?)

EU-US privacy Shield

"safeguards on U.S. government access to data" "effective protection and redress for individuals;" Not sure what I think on this really, I hate the US's spy state, but how are they enforcing this in the US. Doubt the voters in the US had any say in this.

Legal reasons to gather data

"Where the individual concerned, (the 'data subject'), has unambiguously given his or her consent, after being adequately informed;" I like this one a lot, but I hope 'unambiguous consent' applies to when someone hides something 10 pages into a EULA that your forfeit all rights to your personal information, permanently.

"if data processing is needed for a contract, for example, for billing, a job application or a loan request; or" "if processing is required by a legal obligation; or" Um... okay, not quite sure on this since it seems like it can be abused, but I can't quantify how. "if processing is necessary in order to protect the vital interest of the data subject, for example, processing of medical data of a victim of a car accident; or" Okay, so that makes sense if the person is injured and unable to give consent, but this is vague enough to give me some doubt upon what 'vital interest' is and when it can be applied. See cons for more details.

Personal Data Protection

"Personal Data must be processed legally and fairly" Okay, this is actually both common sense but yet extremely ambiguous. Without further explanation, I feel like this could be abused, but since I am saying this here, I won't put it in the cons section.

"It must be collected for explicit and legitimate purposes and used accordingly" "It must be adequate, relevant and not excessive in relation to the purposes for which it is collected and/or further processed" "It must be accurate, and updated where necessary" "Data controllers must ensure that data subjects can rectify, remove or block incorrect data about themselves" "Data that identifies individuals (personal data) must not be kept any longer than strictly necessary" "Data controllers must protect personal data against accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration and disclosure, particularly when processing involves data transmission over networks. They shall implement the appropriate security measures" "These protection measures must ensure a level of protection appropriate to the data." The points immediately above makes sense in one way or another from either a cybresecurity perspective, or just common sense 'why do we need to keep this info we will never use again' perspective.

Handling complaints

They at least try to give power to individuals? I don't know. Most likely it is just an illusion of power but I am trying to give this the benefit of the doubt. "the data controller should cooperate with the supervisory body and the data subject by investigating complaints and redressing any legitimate grievances. If the data concerned is found to be inaccurate or to have been unlawfully obtained, the data subject has the right to demand that it be corrected, blocked or erased." This could be helpful for people who are being defamed through false accusations and/or bad media.

Cons

EU-US Privacy Shield

"strong data protection obligations on companies receiving personal data from the EU" Looks like the legislation can bubble over into US without voter consent.

"annual joint review to monitor the implementation." (I.E. more bureaucratic overhead)

Personal Data Protection

Look at the entry I made in the pro's section and see all the things that a company has to keep in mind. This is a lot, and they are subject to severe penalties if the overlook just one thing and get caught

Handling complaints

"If a data subject believes that his/her rights have been breached or that his/her data has been compromised, he/she has the right to request the data controller to remedy the situation." LMAO like a big corp is going to care what an individual has to say about this. You're so funny EU.

"If the complainant does not receive an adequate answer from the data controller, he/she can file a complaint to one of the national supervisory data protection authorities set up under the Directive LMAO how long will it take for these bureaucratic authorities to respond? Will they respond? How long will it take from when the finally do respond (if they do) until the matter has been resolved? I mean, this is going to be an authority responding to requests from ALL over the EU unless you have dozens of offices spread across the entire continent. This will cost a TON of money to acquire and maintain the people's wages, land, buildings, permits, office supplies, diversity classes, etc. How is this going to be funded? Raise the taxes? Go deeper into debt. How about we make a minimum 20 euro fine for transgressors to pay for it?

"The data controller should cooperate with the supervisory body and the data subject by investigating complaints and redressing any legitimate grievances. If the data concerned is found to be inaccurate or to have been unlawfully obtained, the data subject has the right to demand that it be corrected, blocked or erased." This could be easily appropriated to apply to a private individual and/or small businesses whose political views you don't agree with. Here's a suggestion to you, EU, how about instead of trying to handle all these complaints yourself, why don't you remove legislation protecting companies who abuse people's data? This will give more power to the individuals so they can win lawsuits in court. They win lawsuits, the companies take down the data, and you skim money off of the sum awarded to the winner without having to lift a finger (I know nothing of European courts and how they differ from country to country, so maybe this won't work, but at least it actually might help individuals.)

Legal reasons to gather data

"if processing is necessary in order to protect the vital interest of the data subject, for example, processing of medical data of a victim of a car accident; or" So, 'vital interest' is vague. Extremely vague. When does it apply? What are its conditions? I am sure that they are laid out in more detail in the actual legislation, but it seems like 'vital interest' could easily be twisted around to gathering data about what one's political and life perspectives so their opinions can be changed to the correct ones. Bit extreme, but it serves as an example. **

[These last two. I knew, just knew some kind of backsliding like this would happen. These aren't just are cons, they completely undermine everything this piece of regulation wishes to accomplish, and most condemningly of all, this was said in the exact same breath as the 'pros' which I listed in the previous 'legal reasons' section.]** "if processing is necessary to perform tasks of public interests or tasks carried out by government, tax authorities, the police or other public bodies; or" Of course, OF COURSE the EU would be exempt from this, just as they are exempt from pretty much every other thing which they try to legislate. The phrase 'tasks carried out by the government' is a catch all phrase. Government planning an assassination of a right-winger, well, that's a task carried out by the government.

"if the data controller or a third party has a legitimate interest in doing so, as long as this interest does not affect the interests of the data subject, or infringe on his or her fundamental rights, in particular the right to privacy. This provision establishes the need to strike a reasonable balance between the data controllers' business interests and the privacy of data subjects." Again, of course. This right here completely destroys a huge portion of power that this regulation might have. Leave it to the EU to create yet another massive piece of legislation supposedly to do one thing while leaving a nice little opt out for the EXACT thing that they are trying to stop. I don't know if this is incompetence, power leveraging, or both.

"If the data controller [...] has a legitimate interest in doing so" Okay, so Google has a legitimate interest of knowing the contents of your entire hard drive so it can tailor ads to you as an individual.

"as long as this interest does not affect the interests of the data subject or infringe upon his or her fundamental rights, in particular privacy" But it's anonymous data, they could say. And your privacy isn't breached since it's never viewed by a person, just computer algorithms. The computer doesn't know or care who you are.
EU Online Personal Data Privacy Regulations - Freedom for individuals, or more power to the EU?
